## Introduction

In this project, you will play the role of a Hollywood development executive; 
that is, you are the executive in charge of coming up with new movie ideas. 
Historically, development executives would source the 'life rights' necessary to
make “based on a true story” movies, would secure production options on 
promising new novels, and would partner with owners of established intellectual 
property (IP) to develop movie adaptations. Recently, however, the development 
process has been criticized by Hollywood insiders and audiences alike for 
over-reliance on rote sequels. Our goal is to develop a set of data-driven ideas
for new movies. Before doing so, however, we will dive into Hollywood history to
identify key characteristics of successful movies, to identify successful 
filmmakers and actors, and to examine some of Hollywood's most famous flops.

### Course Context {#context}

#### STA9750

STA9750, the course from which this lesson was adapted, is a core requirement
of the 
[MS in Statistics](https://zicklin.baruch.cuny.edu/academic-programs/graduate/ms/statistics/) 
and 
[MS in Quantitative Methods & Modeling (QMM)](https://zicklin.baruch.cuny.edu/academic-programs/graduate/ms/quantitative-methods-modeling/)
programs offered by the Department of Information Systems and Statistics (ISS)
within the Zicklin School. STA9750 is also an elective commonly taken by students in 
our [MS in Business Analytics and AI](https://zicklin.baruch.cuny.edu/academic-programs/graduate/ms/masters-in-ai-and-business-analytics/)
program and 'analytics-flavored' tracks in other Zicklin programs. 
This is an *intense* one-semester course that teaches students the most 
important computational tools for working data scientists and business 
analysts. 

In our LLM moment, STA9750 has been restructured as an 'applied data analysis' 
course, focusing on the habits and practices of effective data analysis and
de-emphasizing traditional 'programming' fundamentals. As the marginal cost
of *writing* code decreases, the relative value of *verification* and 
*interpretation* has increased. To that end, I take an 'AI Positive' posture,
allowing students full access to any (free-tier) LLM for the 'code-writing'
portions of the assignments. Because they have access to these tools, I in 
turn expect much more from them than I would have 10 years ago. In general, 
students seem to appreciate this Faustian bargain that I have thrust upon 
them[^faust]; for the instructor, it certainly is more rewarding (and more 
exhausting) than teaching basic programming.

[^faust]: You would be correct to note that calling this 'Faustian' when 
students have no say in my expectations breaks the metaphor. I am a STEM 
professor; you get what you pay for. 😈

This assignment is adapted from the second of four 'mini-projects' that replace
traditional homework. In each of these, I work students through a full
'soup-to-nuts' data analysis project; early in the semester, I handle most
of the steps for them, leaving only the final analysis and write-up for them
to handle. As the semester progresses, I progressively remove this 
scaffolding and give them ownership of more and more of the 'data science
workflow'. Ultimately, this is intended to demonstrate the practices I encourage
(and expect) them to use for their final project (in lieu of a traditional exam).

For this assignment, students are responsible for the final three stages of
the data science workflow: 

+---------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
|               | Contents                                   | Student Responsibility in this Project | Students Assume Responsibility |
+:=============:+:==========================================:+:======================================:+:===============================+
| **Step #01**  | Data Identification & Evaluation           |                                        | Final Project                  |
+---------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Step #02**  | Data Acquisition & Cleaning                |                                        | Mini-Project #04               |
+---------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Step #03**  | Exploratory Analysis & Visualization       |                                        | Mini-Project #03               |
+---------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Step #04**  | Combination & Alignment                    | **✓**                                  | Mini-Project #02               |
+---------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Step #05**  | Descriptive and Inferential Analysis       | **✓**                                  | Mini-Project #01               |
+---------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| **Step #06**  | Communication and Presentation of Findings | **✓**                                  | Mini-Project #01               |
+---------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+--------------------------------+


: Students' Responsibilities in the Data Science Workflow. Note that these steps
are not 'one way' and exploratory analysis will occur both before and after
combining data, visualization will be used to interpret analytical results, 
*etc.* {.hover}

#### `JOIN`ing Data Sources

::: {.callout-caution title="Learning Objectives" collapse="true"}

The new learning objectives of this assignment are centered on *combining* data
from different tables to allow novel insights that cannot be gleaned from any 
individual data source. By this point, students have already developed their
skills manipulating data that has already been combined into one table, though
they will build upon those skills in the later portions of this assignment. 

If you 'speak database', this assignment basically covers SQL `JOIN` statements;
it follows a 'single-table' lesson covering the `R` equivalent of 
`SELECT`, `GROUP BY`, `WHERE/HAVING`, and their kin. 

:::


At this point, students are familiar with the ideas of `keys` as a (hopefully) 
unique identifier within a data set. A prior in-class discussion has discussed
examples of ID which are designed for use (*e.g.*, CUNY EmplID) and those 
which are 'good enough' in a limited context (first name within a small class).
We have also discussed how _changing scope_ makes a formerly great ID 
insufficient (*e.g.*, EmplID is a sufficient ID for post-2000 CUNY students, but 
would not suffice for registrar records (or the development office!) going back 
to the first days of the Free Academy).

Participants in this lesson need to know: 

- A _key_ is a column (or combination of columns) that can be used to 'connect'
  records across different data sources. 
- We want _keys_ to be unique and never missing (all records need a key)
- Bad things happen when non-unique keys are used to combine data sets
- Joining by _identity_ is far more robust than joining by _position_. 

  The first row of my data set may or may not match the first row of your data
  set, but `Student 123456778` is likely to be the same across both.
  
> The key, the whole key, and nothing by the key. So help me Codd.

## Showtime!

### Data Identification {#dsw01}

For this assignment, we will be using data from the 
[Internet Movie Database (IMDB)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMDb), an online
data base of all things cinema. Specifically, we will be using data from their
[Non-Commericial Dataset](https://datasets.imdbws.com/) page. These files
are made freely available by IMDb for non-commercial use.


::: {.callout-caution title="Data Identification"}

I try to use a mix of easily understood data like this (Netflix Top 10, 
Spotify charts, *etc*) and more technical info (BLS statistics, Transit
systems, *etc*) over the semester. Because STA9750 attracts students with
such varied backgrounds, it is important to show them that - wherever they are
going - the skills they develop in this class can be applied. 

In my experience, students want evidence that the skills we want them to develop
are actually useful, but they don't actually demand applications to *whatever
they care about*. Real applications to a real problem-even if not their problem-
suffice.

:::


### Data Acquisition and Cleaning {#dsw02}


::: {.callout-caution title="Show Everything"}

Here, I show students the _entire_ workflow used to download, import, and 
clean up the five data sets that are used in this assignment. While this might
seem overwhelming, I find it is important to expose them to the whole process,
even if they are not responsible for it yet. This has several benefits: 

1) The students will submit a fully executable and reproducible document. It
   will start by automatically downloading the data file (if needed) and finish
   with their final figures and tables. This guarantees that the entire project
   is self-contained and can be read without reference to my original assignment.
   
   For students who want to use projects like this as the basis for a professional
   portfolio, this means their work truly stands on their own two feet.
2) For later assignments, I can refer back to the code I share with them here
   as an example of practices they should follow when they are responsible for
   these initial set up steps. 
3) Psychologically, this makes it clear to students that they are interacting
   with *the real thing*, not a simplified and sanitized 'textbook' version of
   a problem. When there are weirdnesses and inconsistencies, they are just a
   fact of life to be dealt with - not a reason to complain and seek clarification.
   
:::


The following code will automatically download and load these files
into `R`: 

```{r}
#| label: 'imdb_name_basics'
#| message: false 
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
library(tidyverse)
get_imdb_file <- function(fname){
    BASE_URL <- "https://datasets.imdbws.com/"
    fname_ext <- paste0(fname, ".tsv.gz")
    fs::dir_create("data")
    fname <- fs::path("data", fname_ext)
    if(!fs::file_exists(fname)){
        FILE_URL <- paste0(BASE_URL, fname_ext)
        download.file(FILE_URL, 
                      destfile = fname)
    }
    readr::read_tsv(fname, 
                    lazy=FALSE, 
                    show_col_types=FALSE, 
                    n_max=1000000, # Increase for more accurate results
                                   # We're currently using a subset for speed
                    na="\\N") |>
        mutate(across(ends_with("year"), as.numeric))
}

NAME_BASICS      <- get_imdb_file("name.basics")
```

```{r}
#| label: 'imdb_title_basics'
#| message: false 
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
TITLE_BASICS     <- get_imdb_file("title.basics")
```

```{r}
#| label: 'imdb_title_ratings'
#| message: false 
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
TITLE_RATINGS    <- get_imdb_file("title.ratings")
```

```{r}
#| label: 'imdb_title_crew'
#| message: false 
#| warning: false
#| cache: true
TITLE_CREW       <- get_imdb_file("title.crew")
```

```{r}
#| label: 'imdb_title_principals'
#| message: false 
#| warning: false

TITLE_PRINCIPALS <- get_imdb_file("title.principals")
``` 

#### Data Sub-Sampling

This data is large enough that we're going to need to immediately 
start down-selecting to get to a data set that we can analyze fluidly. For
our `NAME_BASICS` table, we'll restrict our attention to people with at 
least two "known for" credits.[^1]

```{r}
#| label: 'name_basics_filter'
#| cache: true
NAME_BASICS <- NAME_BASICS |> 
    filter(str_count(knownForTitles, ",") > 1)
```

IMDb has a _long_ tail of obscure titles: 

```{r}
#| label: 'title_ratings_tail'
TITLE_RATINGS |>
    ggplot(aes(x=numVotes)) + 
    geom_histogram(bins=30) +
    xlab("Number of IMDB Ratings") + 
    ylab("Number of Titles") + 
    ggtitle("Majority of IMDB Titles Have Less than 100 Ratings") + 
    theme_bw() + 
    scale_x_log10(label=scales::comma) + 
    scale_y_continuous(label=scales::comma)
```

To keep our computers from working too hard, let's throw out any title
with less than 500 ratings. It's not too hard to see that this drops
about 75% of the entire data set: 

```{r}
#| label: 'title_ratings_quantile'
TITLE_RATINGS |>
    pull(numVotes) |>
    quantile()
```

Applying this drop, we significantly reduce the size of our data set:

```{r}
#| label: 'title_ratings_filter'
#| cache: true
TITLE_RATINGS <- TITLE_RATINGS |>
    filter(numVotes >= 500)
```

We want to perform the same filtering on our other `TITLE_*` tables.
This is a rare use for the [`semi_join`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/filter-joins.html).
Recall that a `semi_join` returns only values which have a match,but
doesn't actually add columns. 

```{r}
#| cache: true
#| label: 'title_other_filter'
#| message: false
TITLE_BASICS <- TITLE_BASICS |>
    semi_join(TITLE_RATINGS, 
              join_by(tconst == tconst))

TITLE_CREW <- TITLE_CREW |>
    semi_join(TITLE_RATINGS, 
              join_by(tconst == tconst))

TITLE_PRINCIPALS <- TITLE_PRINCIPALS |>
    semi_join(TITLE_RATINGS, join_by(tconst == tconst))
```

Finally, let's also restrict our attention to movies by filtering the
`TITLE_BASICS` table to rows where `titleType` is `"movie"` and dropping
`short`s, `tvMovie`s, `tvSeries`, `tvShort`s, *etc.* While I doubt that there
are very many adult films with over 500 published reviews, let's also discard
films where `isAdult` is flagged as `TRUE`. 

```{r}
#| label: title_filter_final
#| cache: false
TITLE_BASICS <- TITLE_BASICS |> 
    filter_out(isAdult==1) |> 
    filter(titleType=="movie")|>
    select(-isAdult, -titleType) 
```

At this point, we've filtered down our data _significantly_ and are ready
to begin analysis in earnest. **Note that our sub-sampling may induce some
'dangling' references: some of the people dropped from the `NAME_BASICS`
table may only appear in one famous movie, and we've likely lost their
info.**

At this point, we do have some rows that we would like to clean up: for
certain projects, there may multiple credited directors or writers.[^dga] 
These appear as comma-separated fields in our data files: *e.g.*, we see
this in the `TITLE_CREW` table: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(gt)
TITLE_CREW |> 
    filter(str_detect(directors, ",") | str_detect(writers, ",")) |>
    filter_out(is.na(writers)) |>
    slice_head(n=10) |>
    gt(id="tbl_crew_comma") |>
    cols_label(tconst="Title ID", 
               directors="Director(s)",
               writers="Writer(s)") |>
    tab_header("Selected Titles with Multiple Directors or Writers")
```

We can use the `separate_longer_delim()` function from the `tidyr` package
to split these up as follows: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(gt)
TITLE_CREW |> 
    filter(str_detect(directors, ",") | str_detect(writers, ",")) |>
    filter_out(is.na(writers)) |>
    slice_head(n=10) |>
    separate_longer_delim(directors, ",") |>
    separate_longer_delim(writers, ",") |>
    gt(id="tbl_crew_comma") |>
    cols_label(tconst="Title ID", 
               directors="Director(s)",
               writers="Writer(s)") |>
    tab_header("Selected Titles with Multiple Directors or Writers")
```

Note that this creates a **longer** data set than we originally started with
because one title (one row) is transformed to multiple rows. We finish our
pre-processing by applying this function to the `directors` and `writers`
columns of the `TITLE_CREW` table, the `genres` column of the `TITLE_BASICS`
table, and the `knownForTitles` of the `NAME_BASICS` column; here, I'm
creating new 'longer' versions of each table instead of modifying the
old table in place to avoid a difficult class of bugs that arise from having
repeatedly duplicated rows in our primary working tables. [^prof]

```{r}
#| cache: true
#| label: split_delim
TITLE_CREW <- TITLE_CREW |> 
    separate_longer_delim(directors, ",") |>
    separate_longer_delim(writers, ",")

NAME_BASICS_LONGER <- NAME_BASICS |>
    separate_longer_delim(knownForTitles, ",") 

TITLE_BASICS_LONGER <- TITLE_BASICS |> 
    separate_longer_delim(genres, ",") |>
    rename(genre=genres)
```

[^dga]: This is not as common as one might think. To prevent producer abuse,
multiple credits are rather disfavored by the creative unions, especially by the
Directors' Guild. See the [DGA Basic Agreement
§7-208](https://www.dga.org/Contracts/Creative-Rights/Basic-Agreement-Article-7)
for details. 

[^prof]: Arguably, we should apply this to the `primaryProfession` column of
the `NAME_BASICS` table as well, but we won't use that in our subsequent
analysis, so it's safe to ignore for now. 


### Combination and Alignment {#dsw03}

To make the most of this data set, we will need to to **combine** all of the
different tables together. Let's start by taking a look at each table separately. 
As you review these, make sure to take note of the common columns (potential
keys) that can be used to join across tables. 

For each table, I am showing a (random) subset of 20 rows. The column names
are shown at the top of each table, immediately below the table name. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
NAME_BASICS |> 
    slice_sample(n=20) |>
    gt(id="tbl_name_basics") |>
    tab_header("NAME_BASICS")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
TITLE_BASICS |> 
    slice_sample(n=20) |>
    gt(id="tbl_title_basics") |>
    tab_header("TITLE_BASICS")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
TITLE_CREW |> 
    slice_sample(n=20) |>
    gt(id="tbl_title_crew") |>
    tab_header("TITLE_CREW")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
TITLE_RATINGS |> 
    slice_sample(n=20) |>
    gt(id="tbl_title_ratings") |>
    tab_header("TITLE_RATINGS")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
TITLE_PRINCIPALS |> 
    slice_sample(n=20) |>
    gt(id="tbl_title_principals") |>
    tab_header("TITLE_PRINCIPALS")
```

In this case, there are sometimes *several* possible ways to join together a 
pair of tables--for instance, we could connect the `TITLE_CREW` table to the 
`NAME_BASICS` table by aligning *director* or *writer*. The following mental 
checklist will help you maximize the probability that you're using the correct
join for your analyses.[^foolproof]

[^foolproof]: This process isn't fool-proof, but it should cover most use-cases.

::: {.callout-note title="Selecting a Join" collapse="true"}

1.  What two pieces of information am I looking to connect? *Answer(s)*: two
    columns from different tables. (If the columns are already in the same 
    table, you don't need a join.)
2.  What is the common feature(s) I can use to join together these two tables? 
    *Answer(s)*: one or more columns that have corresponding values in each 
    table. It is not required for the columns to have the same name or the exact
    same set of values in both tables. (If there is not a natural pair of 
    combining columns, you might need to introduce a third table to your 
    analyis.)
3.  Join type: 

    a) Do I want to *guarantee* use all of the rows from Table 1, filling in with
       missing values if no corresponding row is found in Table 2? 
    b) Do I want to *guarantee* use all of the rows from Table 2, filling in with
       missing values if no corresponding row is found in Table 1? 
      
    If "yes/yes", you probably want a `full_join`; if "yes/no", you probably want
    a `left_join`; if "no/yes", you probably want a `right_join`; if "no/no", you
    probably want an `inner_join`.
4.  Construct a potential join: 

    ```{r}
    #| eval: false
    JOIN_TYPE(TABLE_1_NAME, 
              TABLE_2_NAME, 
              join_by(TABLE_1_KEY_COLUMN == TABLE_2_KEY_COLUMN))
    ```
    
    Here, replace all values with the answers from your questions above. (We
    are not considering non-equality joins here.)
5.  Run your join and make sure you get no "many-to-many" or "many-to-one" 
    warnings.
6.  Embed your join into your full analysis
   
For example, if we want to answer the question "Who played guitar in which bands?"
using the `band_members` and `band_instruments` tables in the `dplyr` package,
the join-design flowchart would go something like this: 

1.  I want to connect the `plays` column from `band_instruments` to the `band`
    column of `band_members`. 
2.  The common feature ("key") connecting the `band_instruments` and `band_members`
    table is the `name` column, which has the same name and consistent values in 
    both tables. 
3.  a. I am fine dropping rows from the `band_instruments` table if I am unable
       to determine what band someone was a part of. 
    b. I am fine dropping rows from the `band_members` table if I am unable to
       determine what instrument someone played. 
      
    These suggest I want to use an `inner_join`. 
4.  My candidate join is: 
   
    ```{r}
    library(dplyr)
    inner_join(band_members, 
               band_instruments, 
               join_by(name == name))
    ```
5.  This runs without any warnings or other danger signs, so I'm good to proceed.
6.  I can use this join to find one guitarist in my data set with a known band: 

    ```{r}
    library(dplyr)
    inner_join(band_members, 
               band_instruments, 
               join_by(name == name)) |>
        filter(plays == "guitar") 
    ```
    so the one row in our result is John (Lennon) playing guitar in the Beatles.
    Sadly, our datasets were incomplete and we lost track of 
    [Keith Richards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Richards), guitarist in
    the Rolling Stones. 
    
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Question 1: Join Practice"}

Identify the joins necessary to answer the following questions. For each 
question, make sure to clearly justify: 

- What type of join is appropriate (and why)
- Which column(s) should be used for the join. Note that the names may not be 
  the same in each table, so be sure to carefully note the name 
  *in each table* in case they differ.

You do not need to actually answer these, but make sure you know _how_ you might
begin to answer each question. 

1. What titles is the actor Harrison Ford most known for?

2. Who is the most active director (most director credits) in this data set? 

3. Of titles with over 100,000 ratings, what is the most highly rated (highest
   average rating) title in this data set? 

4. Since 2020, what has been the average rating of a movie in the Musical 
   genre? 

*Hint:* It may be useful to create a "map" of which columns map to which tables
before attempting these questions. While these can be [quite
formal](https://duckduckgo.com/?q=sql+schema+map&iax=images&ia=images) and can
be created with specialized software like <http://dbdiagram.io>, even 
some basic sketches on a scratch piece of paper are often quite clarifying.

:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Example Answer 1: Join Practice" collapse="true"}

1.  Because Harrison Ford is a person, we start with the `NAME_BASICS` table. 
    Ideally, we could answer this question by looking at the `knownForTitles`
    column, but this has uninterpretable internal identifiers instead of actual
    names. To translate to actual names, we need to connect to the 
    `TITLE_BASICS` table. In this case, we need to join `knownForTitles` from 
    `NAME_BASICS_LONGER` to `tconst` in `TITLE_BASICS`. Here, I can use the 
    `LONGER` name basics because I don't mind the duplicates - I **want** 
    multiple rows in my answers.
    
    In this case, a standard `inner_join()` is fine. We only are interested
    in the _intersection_ of Harrison Ford's most noteworthy titles and their
    names, so we are fine dropping unmatched values.
    
    ```{webr}
    #| autorun: true
    NAME_BASICS_LONGER |> 
        filter(primaryName == "Harrison Ford", 
               birthYear == 1942 # Make sure to ignore the silent-film era Ford
               ) |>
        inner_join(TITLE_BASICS, 
                   join_by(knownForTitles == tconst)) |>
        select(primaryName, knownForTitles, primaryTitle) 
    ```
   

2.  Director credits can be inferred from the `directors` column of the `TITLE_CREW`
    data set. We want to map this to a name from the `NAME_BASICS` table. To align
    our two tables, we want `TITLE_CREW`'s `directors` to match `NAME_BASICS`'s
    `nconst`. 
    As before, we are only interested in the _intersection_ of these two tables, 
    so an `inner_join()` will suffice. 

    ```{webr}
    #| autorun: true
    TITLE_CREW |> 
        count(directors) |> 
        slice_max(n) |> 
        inner_join(NAME_BASICS_LONGER, 
                   join_by(directors == nconst)) |> 
        select(primaryName, birthYear, deathYear, n_credits=n) |> 
        distinct()
    ```

3. 

4. 

:::





### Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) {#dsw04}

::: {.callout-caution title="Guided Exploration"}

An important skill for students to learn is 'data orienteering', situating
themselves within a new data set. While many approaches to this sort of
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) task have been proposed, my favorite is 
simple: 'ask a bunch of questions and see what you find out.'  I pose warm-up
questions to students to seed ideas for the questions they might ask to produce
their final deliverable. My goal in these is to show students that there isn't
*one* right answer to any meaningful question.

For this demo, I'm keeping these relatively short, but this typically forms
the bulk of the assignment. 

:::

#### Quantifying Success

Our goal is to proposal successful new movies. To do so, we need
a way of measuring the success of a movie given only IMDb ratings.[^3] While
there's no "magic number" for success, it is logical to assume that a
successful project will have both a high average IMDb rating, indicating
quality, and a large number of ratings, indicating broad awareness in the
public. 


::: {.callout-important title="Question 2: Success Metric"}

Design a 'success' measure for IMDb entries, reflecting both quality and
broad popular awareness. 

Validate your success metric as follows: 

1. Choose the top 5-10 movies on your metric and confirm that they were
   indeed box office successes.
2. Choose 3-5 movies with large numbers of IMDb votes that score poorly
   on your success metric and confirm that they are indeed of low quality.
3. Choose a prestige actor or director and confirm that they have many projects
   with high scores on your success metric.
4. Come up with a numerical threshold for a project to be a 'success'; that is,
   determine a value $v$ such that movies above $v$ are all "solid" or better.
   
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Example Answer 2: Success Metric" collapse="true"}

I am a **particularly** avaricious vulture, so my success metric will depend
almost exclusively on box office revenue, which I will proxy with the 
*quantity* of IMDb ratings. I only want to use *quality* to avoid 
'review bombs', where internet hordes rate a movie just to express their 
distaste even if they don't see the film. To be clear, I have no qualms 
whatsoever about producing a film that everyone hates, as long as they pay me to
hate it. 

After a bit of experimentation, the following success score seems to work well:

$$\text{Success} = \frac{\text{Quantity of Ratings}}{1 + e^{-\text{Avg Rating}}}$$

To implement this in code, I need to *join* together my table of movies 
(`TITLE_BASICS`) with my table of ratings (`TITLE_RATINGS`). In this case, the
join is straightforward as I can use the `tconst` column from both tables. An
`inner_join()` works well here since I only am interested in looking at movies
where I actually have sufficient info to compute my success metric. 

This join is easy to implement: 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
TITLE_SUCCESS <- TITLE_BASICS |> 
    select(tconst, primaryTitle, startYear) |> 
    inner_join(TITLE_RATINGS, join_by(tconst == tconst)) |> 
    mutate(success = numVotes / (1 + exp(-averageRating)))
```

From here, we can look at the top-scoring films: 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
TITLE_SUCCESS |> slice_max(success, n=10)
```

I would be proud (of how much money I would make) if I were to produce any of
those films. On the tail end of the spectrum, we see some definite failures: 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
TITLE_SUCCESS |> slice_min(success, n=5)
```

A more robust verification would be to find a movie with a high number of 
ratings (for some reason) but still a (relatively) low success score. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
TITLE_SUCCESS |> filter(numVotes > 100000) |> slice_min(success)
```

Yep - that's a stinker[^haimark]!

To see how this plays out in a career, let's look at Denzel Washington, 
who was recentlycrowned [the greatest actor of the
century](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/movies/greatest-actors-actresses.html#denzel-washington) 
by the New York *Times*. We can pull out his top films: 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
TITLE_SUCCESS |> 
  inner_join(TITLE_PRINCIPALS, join_by(tconst==tconst)) |> 
  inner_join(NAME_BASICS, join_by(nconst==nconst)) |> 
  filter(primaryName == "Denzel Washington") |>
  arrange(desc(success)) |> 
  slice_max(success, n=5)
```

Absolute hits all. And on the other end of the spectrum: 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
TITLE_SUCCESS |> 
  inner_join(TITLE_PRINCIPALS, join_by(tconst==tconst)) |> 
  inner_join(NAME_BASICS, join_by(nconst==nconst)) |> 
  filter(primaryName == "Denzel Washington") |>
  arrange(desc(success)) |> 
  slice_min(success, n=5)
```

Some of these were real flops, but *Mississippi Masala* is a respected classic
among cinephiles, absolutely the sort of thing we would hate to produce. 

If we look at the total career of Denzel, a success bar around 100,000 seems 
correct. This gives us Pelican Brief as our 'lowest performing' success
and [the Siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Siege) as our 'best failure'.

:::


[^haimark]: Perhaps the nadir of all Hollywood: {{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aekfPU0SwNw >}}


#### Examining Success by Genre and Decade

Now that you have a working proxy for success, it's time to look at trends in
success over time 

::: {.callout-important title="Question 3: Picking a Genre"}

Identify a good genre for your next film. You do not need to answer these 
questions precisely, but these are may help guide your thinking. 

-   What was the genre with the most "successes" in each decade? 
-   What genre consistently has the most "successes"? What genre used to 
    reliably produced "successes" and has fallen out of favor? 
-   What genre has produced the most "successes" since 2000? Does it have the
    highest success _rate_ or does it only have a large number of successes
    because there are many productions in that genre? 
-   What genre has become more popular in recent years? 

:::

Based on your findings, select a genre for your next project. Note that you may
wish to avoid an "oversatured" genre; you just need to make the argument that
your proposal is a _good_ investment, not necessarily the most _studio-produced
focus-grouped committee-designed generic satisfying_ choice, so feel free to
lean in to your own artistic preferences, as long as you can make an argument
for them.


::: {.callout-tip title="Example Answer 3: Picking a Genre" collapse="true"}

Inspired by the questions above, I can compute the success rates of different 
genres over the past 25 years: 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
TITLE_BASICS_LONGER |> 
  select(tconst, genre) |>
  inner_join(TITLE_SUCCESS, 
             join_by(tconst==tconst)) |>
  filter(startYear > 2000) |> 
  group_by(genre) |>
  summarize(p_success = mean(success > 100000), 
            n_productions = n(), 
            n_success = sum(success>100000)) |> 
  arrange(desc(p_success))
```

From this, I see a market gap in Sci-Fi films, which are almost as consistently
successful as adventure films, but are produced at about half the rate. 

:::

### Analysis {#dsw05}


::: {.callout-caution title="Scaffold to the End"}

Once students are (hopefully) comfortable working with the data, I walk them
through the rest of the analysis. The questions I ask here are typically 
intentionally a bit vague, giving students the ability to put their own stamp
and express their own preferences in their analysis. By making these vague and
soliciting preferences, I try to ensure that no students have the same answers
at the end of the assignment. Then, when students participate in a 'code review'
cycle, they can compare how they approached an open-ended prompt with their 
peers, instead only looking for binary 'right/wrong' answers. Personal 
preference isn't the only way to make questions open ended, but it seems to
make the point more effectively than other phrasings.

:::

#### The Story

Now that you have found a target genre for your project and have identified
the iconic stories in the genre, you need a story. Like any good development 
executive, *i.e.* soulless Hollywood suit, your first instinct should 
be to produce a remake of a classic film in the genre. 

::: {.callout-important title="Question 4: Finding a Classic Movie to Remake"}

Find a classic movie to remake with your key talent. The original should have
a large number of IMDb ratings, a high average rating, and not have been remade
in the past 25 years.[^4] 

:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Example Answer 4: Finding a Classic Movie to Remake" collapse="true"}

Given my analysis above, I have decided to remake a classic Sci-Fi film: I'll
use a similar join strategy as the previous question to get a set of
all-time Sci-Fi greats. Here, I've grouped movies by `primaryTitle` (to identify
potential remakes) and recorded the highest success score ever for that film
and the highest (latest) year in which it was (re-)made: 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
TITLE_BASICS |> 
    select(tconst, genres) |>
    inner_join(TITLE_SUCCESS, 
               join_by(tconst==tconst)) |>
    filter(str_detect(genres, "Sci-Fi")) |> 
    group_by(primaryTitle) |> 
    summarize(max_success = max(success), 
              latest_made = max(startYear), 
              versions=n()) |> 
    arrange(desc(max_success))
```

From these, I see several potential films last made pre-2000. Of them, *The 
Matrix* was the most successful, but it has had some follow-ups so we don't
want to touch it; same for *Empire Strikes Back*. This leaves 
*Back to the Future* as our film to remake.

:::

Once you have found your classic movie to remake, confirm whether key actors,
directors, or writers from the original are still alive. If so, you need to 
contact your legal department to ensure they can secure the rights to the 
project. You may also want to include the classic actors as fan service.


#### The Director

To get the ball rolling, you next want to line up some behind-the-camera talent
for your production. Because directors are the hardest to recruit to a 
project[^post] and have strong opinions about the rest of the behind-the-camera
crew, you are going to first identify a director to helm your film. You are new
to the whole development game, so you plan on hiring a 'bankable' director who
can't miss in the genre: think Fincher in thrillers or Del Toro in Dark Fantasy.

[^post]: A director is typically on a film from pre-production all the way to 
determining the final cut at the end of post-production; this can result in
a time commitment that is _years_ longer than the actors. 

::: {.callout-important title="Question 5: Finding Direction"}

Identify a director for your film. This should be someone with a 
track-record of successful films in your chosen genre. Ideally, they will not
have worked in your genre recently - perhaps having a flop in a different genre 
- and you will be able to market your film as a 'triumphant return to form'.

:::



::: {.callout-tip title="Example Answer 5: Finding Direction" collapse="true"}

Given the above, we want to find the most successful sci-fi directors. This 
requires a more complex join than what we have seen so far: we need to connect

- `TITLE_SUCCESS` to get our success metric
- `TITLE_BASICS` to get genre info
- `TITLE_CREW` to get director IDs
- `NAME_BASICS` to get director names

The only way we can keep our religion here is to work with `inner_join()` 
throughout, ensuring that we get only those films for which we have 
all four pieces of information before we go hunting for our top directors. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
SCIFI_HISTORY_DIRECTORS <- TITLE_BASICS |> 
    select(tconst, genres) |>
    inner_join(TITLE_SUCCESS, 
               join_by(tconst==tconst)) |>
    inner_join(TITLE_CREW, 
               join_by(tconst==tconst)) |>
    inner_join(NAME_BASICS, 
               join_by(directors==nconst)) |>
    mutate(scifi = str_detect(genres,"Sci-Fi")) |>
    group_by(primaryName, scifi) |>
    summarize(n_films = n(), 
              latest = max(startYear), 
              average_success = mean(success)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    pivot_wider(id_cols=primaryName, 
                names_from=scifi, 
                values_from=c(n_films, latest, average_success), 
                names_glue="{.value}_scifi_{scifi}", 
                values_fill=0)
```

That one is quite a lot to chew on, so let's do a bit of work to polish up 
the presentation of our top sci-fi directors. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
SCIFI_HISTORY_DIRECTORS |> 
    filter(average_success_scifi_TRUE > 700000, 
           latest_scifi_TRUE < 2020) |>
    arrange(desc(average_success_scifi_TRUE / average_success_scifi_FALSE)) |>
    gt(id="tbl_top_directors") |>
    cols_label(primaryName="Director Name") |> 
    tab_header("Top Sci-Fi Directors") |>
    tab_spanner(
        label="Sci-Fi",
        columns=ends_with("_TRUE")) |>
    tab_spanner(
        label="NonSci-Fi",
        columns=ends_with("_FALSE")) |>
    cols_label(
        contains("n_films") ~ "Number of Films",
        contains("latest") ~ "Latest Film", 
        contains("average") ~ "Average Success Score"
    )
```

From this, it seems that Michel Gondry would benefit from a return to
his Sci-Fi glory days of *Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind*, a film
which has been remarkably more successful than most of what he produced
in the 20 following years.

:::

#### Star Power

To round out your production, you need to identify two leading actors or
actresses for your film. While you selected a director who would bring 
credibility in the genre, for your stars, you are looking to identify
major talent who have never acted in that sort of film.[^walter]

::: {.callout-important title="Question 6: Star Light, Star Bright"}

Identify two stars with multiple credits to their name to take the leading roles
in your film. These should be actors with a strong track record of success 
who have not worked in your chosen genre before. As you identify your actors, 
consider whether you want a pair of greats coming together for the first
time or whether you want a well-established duo. Similarly, do you want a 
'quality guaranteed' actor-director pairing or something never before seen?

:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Example Answer 6: Star Light, Star Bright" collapse="true"}

To cast our remake of *Back to the Future*, we need to identify a Doc Brown
and a Marty McFly. For Doc Brown, we want a well-known and well-loved actor
with a limited sci-fi resume. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
NO_SCIFI_HISTORY_ACTORS <- TITLE_BASICS |> 
    select(tconst, genres) |>
    inner_join(TITLE_SUCCESS, 
               join_by(tconst==tconst)) |>
    inner_join(TITLE_PRINCIPALS, 
               join_by(tconst==tconst)) |>
    inner_join(NAME_BASICS, 
               join_by(nconst==nconst)) |>
    mutate(scifi = str_detect(genres,"Sci-Fi")) |>
    group_by(primaryName) |>
    filter_out(any(scifi)) |> 
    summarize(n_films = n(), 
              first = min(startYear),
              latest = max(startYear), 
              average_success = mean(success))

NO_SCIFI_HISTORY_ACTORS |>
    filter(n_films > 20) |>
    slice_max(average_success, n=10) |>
    gt(id="tbl_top_actors_doc") |>
    cols_label(
        primaryName="Actor for Doc Brown",
        n_films="Number of Major Acting Credits",
        latest="Latest Credit",
        average_success="Average Success"
    ) |>
    cols_hide(first)
```

It's clear that Canadian icon, Mr. Mike Myers, is the optimal Doc Brown for
our remake, with Tom Hanks as a worthy backup. 

For Marty McFly, we want a new face on the scene, with only a few credits, but
a strong track record.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
NO_SCIFI_HISTORY_ACTORS |> 
    slice_max(first) |>
    gt(id="tbl_top_actors_marty") |>
    cols_label(primaryName="Actor for Marty McFly", 
               n_films="Number of Major Acting Credits",
               first="Film Debut", 
               average_success="Average Success") |>
    cols_hide(latest)
```

There's only one choice!

At this point, our choice to use only a small subset of the data to ensure
everything runs in browser might be coming back to bite us. 

:::


[^walter]: Best case scenario, you're hoping for a Brian Cranston situation: 
Hal Wilkerson (*Malcom in the Middle*) to Walter White (*Breaking Bad*). You
have carefully expunged *the Number 23* and *Stop! or my Mom will Shoot* from
your mind. 

    [![Stallone fell from grace like a Rock(y)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/a/ae/Momshootposter.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop!_Or_My_Mom_Will_Shoot)

### Presentation of Findings {#dsw06}


::: {.callout-info title="Question 7: Write and Deliver Your Pitch"}

Now that you have completed your analysis, write an "elevator pitch" of 
approximately 200-250 words for your proposed Hollywood project. This is the
pitch you will bring to the studio head (your boss); if the studio head likes
your pitch, you will be given a small sum of money to start securing the story
rights and locking down tentative deals with key talent. 

If your boss approves the pitch, you will need to have a brief trailer ready
for the next quarterly earnings call. The marketing department has asked that
you prepare a classic 90's style teaser for them. Adapt the following
cliched formula for your pitch. 

> From director D, the visionary mind between N1; and
> From actor A, beloved star of N2; and
> From actor A2, Hollywood icon of genre G,
> Comes the timeless tail N3
> A story of TOPIC, TOPIC, and TOPIC
> Coming soon to a theater near you. 

If you're creatively-minded, you could have some fun here using
Generative tools to draft a script or mock up a movie poster for your
pitch.

:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Example Answer 7: Write and Deliver Your Pitch" collapse="true"}

![Generated using Google Gemini](./poster.jpg)

What? It's scientifically optimal!

## General Remarks

As you approach this project, recall there are no right or wrong answers. You
are exploring data looking for _exciting_ and _actionable_ findings. You have
several key decisions to make and you can support them with data, but the
decisions are ultimately yours. This project is an exercise both in
the "nuts-and-bolts" of analyzing a large data set and in using data to inform
and refine what is ultimately still a "gut feeling" qualitative business
decision. 

As you iterate on this project, you will see that seemingly small different
choices can produce very different results. That's ok! As data analysts, we
are constantly faced with small and essentially arbitrary decisions. An 
important "meta-skill" is knowing which of these decisions radically
change our findings and which are meaningless. (An arbitrary decision
with no impact on the bottom line is harmless; an arbitrary decision
that could entirely change the plan for the next ten years is a problem.)
Our responsibility is to _clearly_ communicate these choices to our partners
and clients: then we can receive their feedback on which way they would like
to proceed. 

Working in tools like `Quarto` and `R` helps here: if
we provide clean and reproducible code, it should be easy to modify to see
how our final conclusions are changed. Graphics also play an essential role
in this form of clear communication: a 'point estimate' like "Action A is
the best" is far less interpretable than a chart showing the predicted outcomes
of several different actions. 

As you approach this project, focus on justifying and communicating the choices
you make. Structure your argument to communicate both key findings and 
uncertainties around them. Think about how you can use both document structure
(headings vs subsections) and graphics to communicate with both clarity and nuance. 

Good luck!
